title: Kibeho (Rwanda)
hookLine: visions in the 1980s that were later read as warnings before the genocide

lines: SCENES PEOPLE LATER LOOKED BACK AT.
cards: Nyina wa Jambo. In Kinyarwanda, the language of Rwanda, that means Mother of the Word. It's the name schoolgirls at a boarding school in the village of Kibeho said a lady gave herself when she appeared to them.
Their classmates mocked them. Teachers doubted them. Crowds came to watch them in their visions, some believers, others not.
And among the things the young women described were scenes so dark that, years later, people in Rwanda looked back at them and shivered.

teach.b: Begin with the name. Mother of the Word points to the opening of John's Gospel, where the Word is with God in the beginning, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
To call Mary Mother of the Word is to say who she is entirely through her son. Then the message.

By the young women's accounts, the lady asked for prayer and conversion, for hearts turned back to God before it was too late. She asked them to pray the rosary of the Seven Sorrows, which walks through Mary's griefs.
Then the darkness. In one vision, by the accounts, they saw terrible things: rivers of blood, people killing one another, bodies left unburied. They wept as they described it.
Later, Rwanda went through the genocide against the Tutsi, and Kibeho itself became a place of killing.
Afterward, people came to read those visions as warnings that had come before. No one is required to read them that way; it's a reading made looking back.
The Church studied the visions carefully and recognized some of them. Last, the sorrow.
Kibeho today has a shrine to Our Lady of Sorrows, a place of pilgrimage and of mourning.
Matthew's Gospel, telling of children killed in Bethlehem, borrows a prophet's line: "Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not."
The Gospel doesn't explain that grief away, and a shrine of sorrows doesn't either.

how: Catholics honor Our Lady of Kibeho at the Shrine of Our Lady of Sorrows in Kibeho, Rwanda, where pilgrims pray, often using the rosary of the Seven Sorrows the visionaries said Mary asked for, and remember those killed in the genocide.

games.q: you're the local bishop. schoolgirls report visions of Mary, and some of what they describe is terrifying. what do you do?
o: study them carefully before deciding anything.
forbid anyone to speak of them.
games.why: the Church studied the visions carefully, recognized some of them, and, as with every apparition, required no one to believe them.

practice: Hold Rwanda in mind, its hills, its villages, its people today, and then the ones who survived and still carry what they lost, the ones working slowly to live beside neighbors again, the ones never mourned by name.
Don't hurry past the heaviness. If you pray, say a Hail Mary for Rwanda or pray one of the Seven Sorrows; if not, simply hold its people gently.
And if this stirs a grief too heavy to hold, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
